issues.text: UK specialists advise pausing it every 3 months to check it still helps.
issues.problem: Misattribution. The 3-monthly pause is UK prescribing advice (BNF 2010 as reported by Cochrane). The 'specialist' review (Rabbitt 2016, Age Ageing) is by geriatricians in Galway, Ireland, and says only: restrict to severe symptoms, review regularly, discuss risks and benefits.
issues.source_says: Rabbitt 2016 affiliations: Galway University Hospitals, Ireland. Cochrane 2015 Discussion: the BNF (2010) advises interrupting treatment every 3 months.
issues.replacement: UK prescribing advice is to pause it every 3 months to check it still helps.

issues.problem: Same misattribution. Rabbitt 2016 is Irish, and points 2 and 3 (4 weeks, 3-monthly pause) come from the BNF 2010 as reported in the Cochrane review, not from specialists.
issues.source_says: See C10-03-d: Rabbitt gives the severe-only, regular review and discussion advice; BNF 2010 via Cochrane gives the 4-week and 3-monthly advice.
issues.replacement: What the advice says (a review by specialists in older people's medicine, and UK prescribing advice reported in a Cochrane review):

issues.text: Specialist advice is to keep it for severe cramps and pause it every 3 months to check it still helps.
issues.problem: Merges two sources: the 3-monthly pause is UK prescribing advice (BNF 2010), not the specialist review.
issues.replacement: Specialist advice is to keep it for severe cramps and review it regularly; UK prescribing advice is to pause it every 3 months to check it still helps.

issues.text: In trials it cut cramps from about 9 to 6 or 7 a fortnight, with rare serious harms. Advice is to pause it every 3 months to check it helps; many people stop without a clear rise in cramps.
issues.problem: The 'low quality evidence' qualification is dropped, and 'many people stop' overstates the trial finding (26.5 percentage points more had stopped at 12 weeks; the cramp comparison was uncertain).
issues.source_says: Cochrane: low quality evidence. Coppin 2005: 26.5% more stopped; no significant difference in cramps (wide CI).
issues.replacement: In trials it cut cramps from about 9 to 6 or 7 a fortnight (low-quality evidence), with rare serious harms. UK advice is to pause it every 3 months; in one trial, advice to stop did not show a clear rise in cramps.

issues.text: Many people with marked changes have little pain. Many with knee pain have fairly normal X-rays.
issues.problem: 'Marked' is stronger than the source. Bedson and Croft describe radiographic OA in general, and Neogi shows severe (KL grade 4) changes are strongly associated with pain. The claim record wording is 'arthritis changes'.
issues.source_says: Bedson 2008: in those with radiographic knee OA the proportion with pain ranged from 15% to 81%. Neogi 2009: KL 4 vs 0 OR for pain 151 (MOST).
issues.replacement: Many people with arthritis changes on the X-ray have little pain. Many with knee pain have fairly normal X-rays.

issues.text: Many people with marked changes have little pain, and the reverse.
issues.problem: 'Marked' overstates the source, as on the visual.
issues.replacement: Many people with arthritis changes on the X-ray have little pain, and the reverse.

issues.text: Many people with marked X-ray changes have little pain
issues.replacement: Many people with arthritis changes on the X-ray have little pain

issues.text: all described their knee as 'bone on bone', and many had set exercise aside for fear of damage.
issues.problem: Links avoidance to a single motive, and does not say that this small qualitative study shows beliefs, not cause.
issues.source_says: Bunzli 2019: most believed loading could damage the joint; many avoided exercise. Qualitative, 27 people, one hospital.
issues.replacement: all described their knee as 'bone on bone'. Many believed exercise could damage the joint, and many had set it aside. A small study of beliefs, not proof of cause.

issues.text: Few older people were included. We would not start it for sciatica, and would review it.
issues.problem: 'Few older people' is not quantified in the source (mean age 52 to 55, SD about 16 to 17). The opinion is stated as a first-person practice claim without the 'judgement' framing the other versions use.
issues.source_says: Enke 2018 Table 1: mean age 52.4 and 55.2 years; creatinine clearance below 60 ml/min excluded.
issues.replacement: Average age was early to mid 50s. In our judgement, it should not be started for sciatica, and existing prescriptions deserve review.

issues.text: No troublesome pain reported: about 87 in 100
issues.problem: The complement is presented as a finding. The authors rated confidence as low and think true figures are higher because of loss to follow-up, so '87 in 100 without pain' is too confident.
issues.source_says: Cheng 2025: 12.6% (95% CrI 9.9% to 15.9%) at 12 months; low confidence because of substantial loss to follow-up.
issues.replacement: Other 87 in 100: did not report troublesome pain in these studies

issues.text: Studies defined troublesome pain in different ways, and the authors think the true figures are probably higher
issues.replacement: Studies defined troublesome pain in different ways, the authors rated their confidence as low, and they think the true figures are probably higher

issues.text: Roughly twice the rate, still uncommon, and observational.
issues.problem: Drops the wide uncertainty qualification (adjusted HR 2.05, 95% CI 1.08 to 3.86) and the all-ages population.
issues.source_says: Fournier 2015: 4.6 (2.4 to 8.0) vs 1.9 (1.4 to 2.5) per 10,000 person-months; adults of all ages.
issues.replacement: Roughly twice the rate, with wide uncertainty; still uncommon, in adults of all ages, and observational.

issues.text: no pain when sitting and relief on bending forward were the strongest single pointers to lumbar spinal stenosis
issues.problem: Drops the required qualification that the estimates come mostly from specialist clinics.
issues.replacement: no pain when sitting and relief on bending forward were the strongest single pointers to lumbar spinal stenosis (mostly in specialist clinics)
